To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the perceptual strategies that children used to select and organize consonants for the production of 2-syllabic and longer polysyllabic words varied as a function of the word factors of stress and syllable position, and (b ) children's perceptual strategies for selecting consonants from 2-syl- lable words and from longer polysyllabic models with one major stress level were similar.
the perceptual strategies for selecting and organizing consonants from polysyallabic lexical models were related to the number and distribution of stress levels within a word.

(a) primary-stress level was the most important perceptual processing cue for selecting consonants from polysyl-labic lexical models; (b) secondary-stress level was a processing cue that facilitated consonant selection when the model contained one major stress; (c) serial position was a processing cue when the model contained two major stresses, but the cue was not equally effective for both children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which perceptual cues are utilized by the young child in his/her attempts to replicate polysyllabic lexical stimuli.
the development of the ability to select, organize, and replicate the consonantal structure of polysyllabic lexical items.
the perceptual processes that underlie the development of productive strategies in early language development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the perceptual processing strategies for selecting and organizing consonants from polysylabic words are closely related to the child's own productive repertoire of syllables.
perceptual strategies for polysyllabic words are related to word factors (stress and serial position), and to the number of phonological segments produced.
perceptual strategies for polysyllabic words are related to the number, location, and type of syllables produced by the child.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
(a) the perceptual strategies for polysyllabic word models are similar for children of the same age and (b) the perceptual strategy of each child appears to be related to his/her production patterns.

(a) perceptual processing strategies for polysyllabic words are not related to a child's productive strategy, and (b), in the early stages of language development, perceptual processing strategies appear to be closely related, if not identical, to the strategies of children who produce the same word.
the perceptual strategies for consonant selection are closely related to the phonological structure of the word.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children's perceptual strategies are consistent and that they are not necessarily related to production patterns.
the perceptual strategies that children use to organize the phonetic information in polysyllabic words are not necessarily the same as the strategies they use to produce the words.
children are not simply "copying" adult speech, but that their production patterns are influenced by their perceptual strategies.
